indicators.title: Grain in storage
indicators.question: Is there more or less grain in the country's elevators and ports than usual for this time of year?
indicators.definition: Wheat, canola and other grains held in licensed grain elevators across the Prairies and at port terminals, as reported each week by the Canadian Grain Commission.
indicators.how_calculated: We add up all grain in storage at the end of the latest week and compare the total with the same week in each of the past five crop years.
indicators.does_not_show: Grain still on farms, which is most of Canada's grain, and food further along the chain. A high number can mean a comfortable reserve, or grain that cannot move. Read it alongside grain shipped through ports.

screen.screens_why: Both matter: how full the elevators are, and how fast they are filling or emptying.
screen.rung_label: Highest or lowest in five years, but moving at its usual pace
screen.rung_means: This reading is the highest or lowest of the comparable years, but it is not moving faster than usual. On a figure that climbs year after year this is the normal state, not a warning.
screen.level_words: It is the highest of the 6 comparable readings: this one and the past 5 years.
screen.level_luck: With 5 years to compare, the highest or lowest reading happens about one year in three by chance alone, even when nothing has changed.
screen.pace_words: It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in each of the past 5 crop years (at least 3 needed). A crop year runs from August to July.

reading.why_for_canada: Grain in licensed elevators and at port terminals is the part of the harvest that is ready to move. When it is high while shipments are low, the grain is stuck rather than saved; when both fall together, Canada is selling well.
reading.what_next: Read it beside the shipment figures. Stocks climbing while shipments fall is what a transport blockage looks like from the elevator end, which is the chain the rail test follows.
reading.to_consider: Ask the railways and the terminals for their own loading plans before the next grain week, and check whether trucking and other ports could take any of the volume if the corridor stays blocked.

indicators.title: Grain shipped through ports
indicators.question: Is grain leaving Canada's ports at a normal pace?
indicators.definition: Grain and oilseeds shipped abroad from port terminals in Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Thunder Bay, the St. Lawrence and elsewhere, reported each week by the Canadian Grain Commission.
indicators.how_calculated: We add up the latest four weeks, because ships arrive unevenly, and compare the total with the same four weeks in each of the past five crop years.
indicators.does_not_show: Why the pace changed. A slowdown can come from rail or port problems, weather, a smaller harvest or weaker sales. Grain sent to the United States by rail or truck is not included.

screen.screens_why: Both matter: the four-week pace against past years, and whether it is falling unusually fast.

indicators.title: Fresh fruit and vegetable prices
indicators.question: Are fresh fruit and vegetable prices unusual for this time of year?
indicators.unit: Canadian dollars per box or bag
indicators.definition: Daily wholesale prices at the Toronto wholesale market for 12 fruits and vegetables, from Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada. Each product is always the same variety, grade, origin and box size, so its price can be compared over time.
indicators.how_calculated: For each product we take the average price in the latest week and compare it with the same week in up to 5 past years. Past prices are first converted to October 2026's dollars using the Consumer Price Index, so inflation alone does not make today's prices look high. A product is flagged only if this week's price is above or below every past year.

indicators.title: Grocery prices compared with wages
indicators.question: Are grocery prices rising faster than what people earn?
indicators.definition: How much grocery prices changed over 12 months (Statistics Canada's Consumer Price Index for food bought in stores), set against how much the average hourly wage changed over the same 12 months (Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey).
indicators.how_calculated: For each month we compare prices and wages with the same month a year earlier. The gap is the difference between the two changes, in percentage points.
indicators.does_not_show: Who is struggling. National averages hide people without wages, such as pensioners and people on income support, differences between regions, and households that spend a larger share of their income on food.

screen.screens_why: Already published as the gap between two rates of change, which can be negative. Neither check is meaningful on such a gap, so it is shown as published. A level check on the gap itself would be worth adding; see the remaining research needs.
screen.rung_label: Not screened
screen.rung_means: This figure is shown as published, without either check. The reason is on its own page.

reading.why_for_canada: People do not experience food prices on their own; they experience them against what they earn. This gap is the closest published figure to whether food is getting harder to afford.
reading.what_next: A gap that stays open for several months tends to show up later in the share of people who cannot afford enough food, which is published only once a year and long after the fact.
reading.to_consider: Check whether income support, school meal and food bank budgets are keeping pace with food prices rather than with general inflation, which has been rising more slowly.

indicators.definition: Estimated tonnes of cargo loaded onto ships each day at Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Montreal, Halifax and Thunder Bay. PortWatch estimates the tonnage from ships' tracking signals and how low they sit in the water.

indicators.title: Stock held by food processors
indicators.question: How much food stock do processors hold against what they are shipping?
indicators.definition: The value of stock held by Canadian food manufacturers at the end of each month, divided by the value of what they shipped that month, from Statistics Canada's monthly survey of manufacturing. A higher figure means more stock sitting between farms and shops.
indicators.how_calculated: We use the figures that are not adjusted for the season, and compare each month with the same month in each of the past five years, because stock levels follow the calendar.
indicators.does_not_show: Days of supply. These are dollars, not tonnes, so the figure also moves when prices move. It covers the whole country and the whole industry, so it says nothing about one plant, one product or one region, and a disruption lasting a week may not show up in a month-end figure at all.

headline.text: In September 2026, food processors held about $0.98 of stock for every dollar of food they shipped that month. Of that, $0.54 was finished food ready to ship. Across all manufacturing the figure was $1.55. It is inside the range of the past five years for this time of year. It is about 4% below the typical level. It is moving at about its usual pace for this time of year.
